extracted.intended_audience: Christian laypeople — especially debtors, tradesmen, shopkeepers, and professing Christians seeking moral instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive Christian moral instructions for debtors, traders, and professing believers: how to avoid fraud, how to behave when insolvent, obligations to creditors and family, and the sinfulness of dishonest trade (false weights/measures and concealment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not defraud thy neighbour / Thou shalt not defraud nor rob
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, nor rob him.” — Defrauding (breaking) is deceit, beguiling, a kind of theft and robbery, done by design with lies and dissimulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats this as a capital moral rule: deliberate plotting, invention, and deceit (leading others to consent while being taken in a deceitful net) constitute a compounded wickedness. Scriptural backing and the Apostle’s warning (God will be the avenger) are cited; the offender imitates the Devil. The passage emphasizes conscience, natural law, and eternal accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: If unable to pay, cease incurring further debt
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let him not run one penny further in his Creditors debt.” — One who knows he cannot pay must not knowingly borrow more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doing so is conscious wrongdoing: ‘The wicked borroweth and payeth not again.’ Continuing to borrow when unable to pay is treated as taking away what is another’s and is condemned by conscience and Scripture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the cause of your indebtedness
rubrics_metrics.description: A debtor should consider how and by what means he came into the condition of not being able to pay — e.g., sloth in calling, extravagant living, lending others what is not his, or the immediate hand/judgment of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes honest self-examination to determine whether poverty arises from personal sin (remissness, extravagance, pride) — in which case repentance is required — or from providence/affliction (in which case submission and humility are called for).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repent when indebted through personal sin (sloth, extravagance, lending away others' goods)
rubrics_metrics.description: If fall into debt through slothfulness in business, lavish diet/apparel, or lending away what is not one’s own, the debtor has sinned against the Lord and must humble himself and repent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats sloth and waste as sins akin to stealing from one’s household: debtor must seek a sense of sin, repent, and correct habits to live quietly and comfortably in conscience moving forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept providential poverty humbly and without murmuring
rubrics_metrics.description: If poverty comes by the immediate hand of God (visible or invisible causes), the debtor should humble himself, consider possible hidden sin, and submit to God’s judgment without repining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poverty may be God changing one’s condition to humble and refine; benefits of low condition are listed (way to exaltation in God’s time; blessings that attend low condition; clearer sight of God’s providence; poor chosen rich in faith). Submission and patience are urged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely disclose condition to creditors and seek to make honest restitution (threefold duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A debtor should timely acquaint his creditors with his condition and do three things: (1) heartily and unfeignedly ask forgiveness; (2) proffer all that he has in the world (hide nothing, strip to his raiment); (3) if those two suffice not, offer his body to be at their disposal (imprisonment or labour) until he has made amends, reserving reasonable support for his poor family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the most honest way: submitting one’s estate and person to creditors, trusting God to incline their hearts. Doing so engages God’s favor and gives true conscience-rest; refusing to do so is persisting in sin and opposing Providence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conceal assets or hinder creditors (no hiding of linen/plate/jewels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealing goods (hiding linen, plate, jewels or other money/goods) to cheat creditors is condemned as deliberate deceit and breaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such concealment is equated with beguiling creditors and is morally blameworthy; full disclosure and offering all one has is the upright alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious profession does not excuse fraud — hypocritical professors must be disowned
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who profess religion yet defraud their neighbours are hypocrites and a scandal to religion; profession does not deliver them from God’s censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument cites apostolic warnings (unrighteous shall not inherit the Kingdom) and exhorts Christians to disown professing deceivers. True profession must be matched by honest conduct; otherwise the profession is a ‘stalking-horse’ for sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest conduct despite misfortune distinguishes the godly from the wicked
rubrics_metrics.description: A godly man who is run out of his estate by unforeseen calamity (fire, thieves, loss of cattle, etc.) despite faithful endeavour is not the same as one who fraudulently breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text allows for providential loss beyond one’s control (like a ship sinking despite the pilot’s skill); such losses call for humble submission rather than moral blame. The debtor’s prior diligence and integrity matter in moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use false weights and measures — a false balance is an abomination
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural injunctions: ‘Do no unrighteousness in...weights or in measures... A false balance is an abomination to the Lord.’ Do not have divers weights/measures (one to buy by, another to sell by).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Old Testament law is cited for exactness in balances/weights; the New Testament’s teaching (good measure pressed down etc.) is invoked to show the rule’s continuing moral force. Using deceitful weights/measures is equated to robbery and oppressing the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: False weights and measures mark the wicked and oppressors
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceitful balances are found in the houses of evildoers, the cruel, and those who love to oppress; they are used to ‘swallow up the needy’ and make the poor fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such practices identify the user as impure and covetous; Scripture promises God will remember and judge those deeds. The moral diagnosis ties economic cheating to cruelty and oppression of the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom is no defence for cheating; conscience governs right dealing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleading ‘custom’ or ‘they gave it me so’ does not excuse using false measures; what is altogether just must be done regardless of how one was treated in buying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text rejects reciprocal cheating as justification. Good conscience, not custom, will help at God’s tribunal; one must not perpetuate wrong even if previously wronged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ill-gotten gain brings no true good — temporal and eternal loss follows deceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Gain got by dishonest means profits not: the wicked’s substance will be cast away; he may seem prosperous briefly but will lose both temporal goods and jeopardize his soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites scripture and Proverbs: wealth of the sinner laid up for the just; gaining the world but losing one’s soul is ultimate loss. The passage warns that deceitful prosperity ends in God’s judgment, loss, and final retribution.
